title: The Morning Brief: US Open final set; Patriots open season in ruins
dek: Elena Rybakina's comeback win over Coco Gauff clinches the world No. 1 ranking and sets up a championship match against Aryna Sabalenka on Sunday, while the Patriots' season opener revealed late-game collapse and cascading injuries that will reshape their stretch ahead.
author: GoCheckMySports
key_fact: Friday's major threads are the consolidation of women's tennis at the top and the Patriots' immediate accountability for a 13-10 loss to Seattle that unfolded as preventable collapse in the final quarter, compounded by injuries to their newly acquired star receiver.
bottom_line: Friday brought the US Open women's final into focus: Rybakina has clinched No. 1 and faces Sabalenka, who leads their head-to-head but has shown vulnerability in hard-court majors late in tournaments. The Patriots' season opened with a fourth-quarter collapse that cost them a game they led 10-0 and will now navigate without their star receiver for at least four weeks. The Clippers investigation moved from league penalties into federal criminal territory, and the Falcons face uncertainty at quarterback with Tagovailoa's status to be clarified by Friday's injury report. Sunday's US Open final and Week 1 NFL games will test whether the patterns established this week hold or reverse.
body: Elena Rybakina rallied from a set down to defeat Coco Gauff 3-6, 6-4, 6-4 in the US Open women's semifinal on Friday and clinched the world No. 1 ranking, ending Aryna Sabalenka's 99-week reign at the top. Rybakina will face Sabalenka in the final on September 14, the first time since 2013 that the top two seeds have contested a US Open women's championship. The semifinal field itself marked the first time in 51 years that all four top seeds reached that stage at the tournament. On hard courts, the pattern is even more recent: the top four seeds have not all reached the semifinals at any major since Wimbledon in 2009, per BBC Sport.

The NFL season opened Thursday with a cautionary tale for New England. The Patriots led Seattle 10-0 deep into the third quarter but surrendered 13 straight points and lost 13-10 in a game that turned on Drake Maye's interception to Seahawks cornerback Josh Jobe in the end zone with 26 seconds remaining. The play occurred with the Patriots at the Seattle 16-yard line on third-and-5, in field-goal range with overtime available. NBC's Cris Collinsworth called the throw indefensible. New England's offense had been effective for most of the afternoon, but Maye threw three interceptions in the fourth quarter alone, a deterioration that begs immediate review before the Patriots face Pittsburgh on September 17. The collapse was compounded by injury: Patriots wide receiver A.J. Brown, the team's marquee receiver acquisition, suffered a high ankle sprain in the third quarter and is expected to miss at least four weeks, leaving Maye without his top target as the team absorbs a season-opening loss that exposed fourth-quarter decision-making under pressure.

Away from the field, two investigations advanced. The U.S. attorney's office in Brooklyn opened a criminal investigation into the Los Angeles Clippers, owner Steve Ballmer, and Kawhi Leonard for alleged salary-cap circumvention via third-party endorsement deals, escalating what was already the NBA's most severe penalty from league enforcement into federal criminal territory. Prosecutors have issued at least one subpoena, and the investigation remains in its earliest stages. Separately, LeShon Johnson, a former running back for the Green Bay Packers, Arizona Cardinals, and New York Giants, was sentenced to five years in federal prison on Thursday for operating a large-scale dogfighting ring in Oklahoma. Johnson, 55, received three years of supervised release and a $30,000 fine; he surrendered 190 dogs to the government, the largest number seized from one individual in a federal dogfighting case according to the Department of Justice.

In baseball's final weeks, roster moves shaped the stretch run. The Dodgers placed Shohei Ohtani on the 15-day injured list to address left knee soreness and right biceps injuries, making him eligible to return September 23 with five regular-season games remaining before the postseason. Manager Dave Roberts said that if it were a playoff game, Ohtani would be in the lineup, but two weeks of rest will position him better for October. The Dodgers also called up Josue De Paula, their top prospect ranked No. 6 on MLB Pipeline's Top 100, to debut as early as Friday in Miami, skipping Triple-A entirely. De Paula, 21, slashed .303/.401/.547 with 27 homers in 124 Double-A games in 2026 and is described by MLB.com as a slightly smaller but more athletic version of Yordan Alvarez. No Dodgers position player has skipped Triple-A under Andrew Friedman's tenure as president of baseball operations.

In the NFL, the Atlanta Falcons face immediate uncertainty at the quarterback position. Tua Tagovailoa suffered an oblique injury during Thursday practice and is listed day-to-day with his availability for Sunday's Week 1 opener against Pittsburgh unclear. If Tagovailoa cannot play, the Falcons would turn to Cooper Rush, who took first-team reps during Thursday practice for the first time since joining Atlanta, or undrafted rookie Jack Strand. Michael Penix Jr., the team's first-round pick, is recovering from left ACL surgery and told coach Kevin Stefanski he does not feel ready for live game action. Meanwhile, the Seattle Seahawks' quarterback situation remains fluid. Sam Darnold exited the season opener with a hip injury on the opening drive; a fracture was ruled out, but further testing was pending. Drew Lock entered for the second drive and completed the 13-10 victory.
